title: The ten-day retreat, day one
hook: what happens: noble silence, early bells, the breath
tomorrow: The ten-day retreat, the hard days

segments.voice: Yesterday, bowing, from palms together to the whole body on the floor. Your line was bow. This week we heard Buddhists chant in Pali, Japanese, Tibetan and Chinese, then lowered the head. Now, a retreat. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-six.

The phone goes into an envelope with your name on it. Someone at a folding table takes it, smiles, and puts it in a box. That evening, after a short talk, a teacher announces that silence begins now. Not just no talking: no notes passed, no waving, no catching anyone's eye across the dining hall. You walk back to a narrow room with a bed and a hook for your coat. The next sound you'll hear is a bell, in the dark, long before the sun. Today begins a short series on the ten-day retreat, starting with day one.
screen: `THE PHONE IN AN ENVELOPE.` → `SILENCE BEGINS NOW.` → `A BELL IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: First, the silence. Retreats often call it noble silence. In courses taught in the tradition of S. N. Goenka, one well-known form of the ten-day retreat, students agree to keep silent with each other, with body as well as voice, for most of the course. The point isn't to be cold. It's to stop performing, so there's no one to explain yourself to, and the mind has fewer places to hide. Second, the bells. A bell wakes the hall before dawn. Bells call people to the meditation hall, to meals, to rest. The day runs on them, so nobody has to decide what to do next. Deciding is one more thing set down. Third, the breath. On day one, the instruction is small: feel the breath as it comes in and goes out, at the nostrils. Not controlling it. Just knowing it. This is very close to the old discourse on mindfulness of breathing, where the Buddha describes a monk going to a quiet place, sitting, and knowing a long breath as long and a short breath as short. Fourth, what day one feels like, by the accounts students give. The mind wanders off everywhere, and the instruction is simply to come back. Then wander, and come back. Teachers on these courses say that is not failing the practice. Coming back is the practice. The ten-day retreat starts with almost nothing: no phone, no talking, and the air at the tip of the nose.
screen: `NOBLE SILENCE: NOTHING TO PERFORM.` · `THE BELLS DECIDE THE DAY.` · `THE BREATH AT THE NOSTRILS.` · `WANDER, AND COME BACK.` · then, large: `DAY ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's a way to try it, if you'd like. First, plan a small retreat day. Pick a morning or an afternoon in the week ahead. Decide when your phone goes in a drawer, an hour without talking or screens, and one sit at a set time. Hold the plan in your mind, simple and doable. Then, for the rest of the sit, try day one's instruction. Feel the air at the nostrils, coming in, going out. When the mind wanders, notice where it went, and come back to the next breath. The bell holds the time.
The ten-day retreat. A stretch of days in silence, run on bells, with long hours of meditation, beginning with nothing more than the breath. Today's word.
Your line: day one. Today, keep one small piece of retreat: the first ten minutes after you wake, no phone, no talking, just the breath. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: On ten-day meditation retreats, such as those in the tradition of S. N. Goenka, students keep noble silence, rise to a bell before dawn, follow a fixed schedule, and begin by attending to the breath at the nostrils.
